A 40-year-old man presented with respiratory compromise and was intubated. After being sent home, he re-presented later that day in respiratory distress, requiring intubation.
His symptoms progressed so rapidly that he required intensive care support on the day of admission, only 1 week after symptom onset.
The family reported a 1-week prodrome of mood change, hallucinations and involuntary tic-like jerks.

After tracheostomy, he was found to have ophthalmoplegia, severe limb rigidity, stimulus-sensitive myoclonus and autonomic dysfunction.

Serum glycine receptor antibodies were strongly positive: we diagnosed progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus.

Despite a relapse, he has done well following immunotherapies.

Despite a relapse, he has done well following immunotherapies.

He gradually responded to treatment, and at 6 months, he was weaned off ventilation and the tracheostomy was removed. His rigidity, spasms and ophthalmoplegia had improved.

We also treated him symptomatically for rigidity with an intrathecal baclofen pump and oral clonazepam.

We gave further plasma exchange, increased the corticosteroid dose, and increased the symptomatic treatments (intrathecal baclofen and clonazepam).

He was discharged from hospital 11 months from disease onset, and remains on prednisolone 20 mg, clonazepam and intrathecal baclofen.
